There is a particular kind of light that arrives in late October, just before the clocks change—low, honeyed, and almost unbearably tender. It spills across kitchen tables and stretches shadows into long blue fingers along sidewalks. I notice it most when I'm doing something ordinary, like washing a dish or tying my shoes, and suddenly the world feels as if it's being held up to the light for inspection, every edge softened, every color deepened. The ordinary becomes monumental for a second: the grain of the wooden counter, the faint dust on a windowsill, the way a spoon catches the sun and throws a small quivering star onto the ceiling.

I used to think that moments like these needed to be captured—photographed, written down, told to someone. But now I suspect they ask for something quieter. They want to be witnessed and then let go, like a breath. The star on the ceiling will tilt and vanish. The light will shift into gray dusk. And that's the point—its brevity is what makes it ache. If it stayed forever, we'd stop seeing it.

There is a strange freedom in allowing things to be temporary. In noticing the last warm day of the year without clinging to it. In loving a person without demanding that they stay the same. In sitting with a feeling—sadness, wonder, longing—and letting it pass through you like weather. The Buddhists have a word for this: impermanence. But it doesn't have to be a lesson. It can just be a fact, like rain, like hunger, like the fact that we will all eventually be someone else's memory.

I think about the people I've known who are gone now—not dead, just elsewhere. The friend who moved across the ocean. The grandfather whose voice I can still hear if I'm quiet. The versions of myself that live in old photographs, squinting into a sun that no longer exists. Each of us is a procession of ghosts, shedding selves like skin. And yet there is something continuous too—a thread of attention, a way of tilting the head when listening, a laugh that hasn't changed since childhood. We are both an archive and a current.

Somewhere, right now, someone is having the same thought. In a city I've never visited, on a rainy street, a person is looking at their hands and wondering what it means to be here, in this particular body, at this particular moment. There is comfort in that—not because we're connected in some mystical way, but simply because it means I'm not alone in the habit of thinking. We are all walking around with completely unique minds, each one a universe that will one day go dark. And yet we make soup for each other. We send voice notes. We leave the porch light on.

Maybe that's what I want to write about, freely, without a plan: the quiet miracle of paying attention. The way a coffee cup feels warm against someone else's fingers. The sound of a page turning in a room where someone else is reading. The small, unheroic gestures that hold our lives together like thread. No great revelations, just a thousand tiny ones, each real and fleeting.

Thank you for reading this. Now go look at the light in your own room. It won't wait.Here's a piece of free writing — a meditation on light, impermanence, and noticing.
